summary_grc: ὁ Κλεινίας τοῖς παισὶ τὴν ἐλαίαν καὶ τὰ σημεῖα τῆς τριαίνης ἐν τῇ ἀκροπόλει δείκνυσιν· οἱ δώδεκα θεοὶ τὴν χώραν τῇ Ἀθηνᾷ κρίνουσιν.
summary_en: On the Acropolis Kleinias shows the children Athena's olive and the marks of Poseidon's trident, and tells how the two gods quarrelled over Attica and the twelve gods judged between them. Paragraphs 2 and 3 adapt Apollodorus 3.14.1.
caption_grc: γενομένης δὲ ἔριδος περὶ τῆς χώρας, ὁ Ζεὺς κριτὰς ἔδωκε τοὺς δώδεκα θεούς.

original.note: Apollodorus, Library 3.14.1, adapted in paragraphs 2 and 3. Apollodorus wrote in the 1st or 2nd century AD, but the story is old Athenian lore: the contest of Athena and Poseidon filled the west pediment of the Parthenon, finished in 432, a few months before our scene. Where Apollodorus says the olive 'is shown now in the Pandroseion', he means his own day.

grammar.md:
**Three habits of the mythographer.** This passage shows three things Apollodorus does on every page.

**1. The genitive absolute sets the scene.** A noun and a participle in the genitive, loosely attached to the sentence, tell you the circumstances before the main action:

| Apollodorus | 'while / when / after …' |
|---|---|
| γενομένης δὲ ἔριδος ἀμφοῖν | when a quarrel arose between the two |
| τούτων δικαζόντων | while these were judging |
| Κέκροπος μαρτυρήσαντος | Kekrops having testified, since Kekrops testified |

Rule of thumb: if a genitive noun + participle comes first and is not governed by anything, it is an absolute; translate with 'when', 'while' or 'since'.

**2. Myths explain what you can still see (aetiology).** A relative clause often ties the story to the present: θάλασσαν, ἣν νῦν Ἐρεχθηίδα καλοῦσι 'a sea, which they now call the Erechtheid'; ἐλαίαν, ἣ νῦν … δείκνυται 'an olive, which is shown now'. The name of the land (Κεκροπία), the city (Ἀθῆναι) and the marks in the rock are all explained by the story.

**3. Other versions.** Apollodorus is a scholar: he tells you when sources disagree. φασίν 'they say'; οὐχ ὡς εἶπόν τινες … 'not, as some have said, Kekrops and Kranaos, but the twelve gods'. Watch for ὡς ἔνιοι λέγουσιν, ὡς δέ τινές φασι: you will need them in the next lessons.

culture.title: The contest on the Parthenon
culture.md:
When our family climbs the Acropolis in 430, the **Parthenon** is brand new: the building was finished in 438 and its sculptures in 432. High on its **west pediment**, the first thing a visitor saw coming up through the gateway, stood the contest itself: Athena and Poseidon springing apart in the centre, the olive between them, chariots and the old kings of Attica, Kekrops among them, on either side (Pausanias 1.24.5). Most of the figures were smashed in 1687; we know the scene from drawings made in 1674 and from vase painters who copied it, such as the painter of a hydria found at Pella.

The story was not only on marble. North of the Parthenon, in the old sanctuary of Athena Polias and Erechtheus (the Erechtheion we know was begun about 421), Athenians were shown **the sacred olive**, **the salt spring** ('the sea') and **marks in the rock** said to be from Poseidon's trident. Herodotus (8.55) says the Persians burned the olive in 480, and the next day the Athenians found a new shoot a cubit long, a sign the city would live. Kleinias, who rowed at Salamis that year, would have heard the story as news.

The myth also says something the Athenians believed about themselves: the olive and the sea, farming and the fleet, both belonged to Athens.
